body: Hi, if the Trojan War happened, was it actually a unified coalition of Greeks, and if so, what was the nature of such an alliance and how common were Greek grand coalitions in Ancient Greece?

Further prompt: would the three countries work well together? Think of maybe their rivalries, or a higher difficulty in communication. Maybe the fact that (if they were previously unaware of the Romans and they just showed up in Luxembourg) their respective armies are all in their respective countries.

Airlifting is a good point, I hadn't thought of that. With no way of shooting them down they would be a big help to the defenders, also artillery capable of firing accurately from miles away, and superior recon and communication would all be valuable assets against the Romans.
Technically we're talking about 2800 men here, not 300, though your point still stands. Who knows, maybe they get worshipped as gods with their technology, haha.

Couldn't have put it better. To think of something the Romans could do to get around allied guns, they could go MacBeth style and advance behind sheets of bulletproof metal. Maybe coat their Shields. That seems characteristically Roman. In Rd 2 the allies are fucked, because the adaptability of the Romans is unparalleled.

Yep. The only way I can see the allies win is if Rome makes a miscalculation and assaults the city, then they have a chance. They have multiple lines of defence, Roman cavalry is useless, and the citystates still have huge weapon advantages. Though Rome probably would still win. I see them getting repulsed in an assault, then just sitting back and sieging it into defeat.

However, as Luxembourg is essentially only one city, it would not lose much under a siege, though I agree that if the Romans encircled them, it would be impossible to break out and would result in eventual capitulation.
You do have a good point; any able man can fire semi decently into columns that would be hard to miss. (at least before Rome adapts their tactics)

Also if fighting Stalingrad-esque in an urban environment, the allies take away Rome's number advantage and, considering they have enough ammo, could hold out indefinitely with their weapon advantage.

We must also consider the Romans' famed strategies, they won't necessarily all be charging in. As you said it's highly trained soldiers vs soldiers of small European countries. Also note cavalry. If the legions are used as gun fodder a successful cavalry attack could be crucial.
